title: A checkpoint remembers progress; a rate limit controls the next bite
goal: Separate ingestion correctness from ingestion capacity so backlog tuning never destroys recovery evidence.
tag: Certification cycle 2 · focused lesson 1 · ingestion and compute evidence
concept:
A deli ticket tells the cook which order comes next. A tray size tells the cook how many sandwiches to carry. One remembers position; the other limits work.

Streaming ingestion needs both ideas. A checkpoint or committed offset remembers durable progress after a crash. A batch-size or client-capacity control bounds how much work enters the next processing interval. Raising the limit can drain a backlog faster, but it does not make progress durable. Deleting progress state can make the system repeat or miss work.
example: Source receipts-59 has 2,500 files. A hard limit of 1,000 files produces batches of 1,000, 1,000, and 500. The checkpoint advances after each committed batch. If batch two fails before commit, recovery resumes from the batch-one checkpoint—not from the configured limit.

use_case.when: Use separate progress and capacity controls when a stream has a backlog or bursty arrivals.
use_case.example: A retail data platform must catch up after an object-store notification outage without replaying already committed receipts.
use_case.decision: Preserve durable progress first. Tune batch or client capacity from memory, latency, cost, and downstream evidence. Never use state expiry as a casual throughput knob.

practice: Change the model between durable progress plus a 1,000-file limit and a limit with lost progress. Predict the retry cursor.
boundary: The local model counts files of equal cost. It does not run cloud discovery, Spark, Snowpipe Streaming, schemas, rejected rows, autoscaling, network limits, warehouse cost, or product recovery.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: offset tokens prove channel progress; they do not size the client
product_sections.html:
First-minute product recall: Complete the scheduled product refresher above.

-- Validation SQL; not executed in SnowflakeSELECT COUNT(*) FROM bronze_receiptsWHERE source_partition = 'p59';# SDK sketch: appendRows(rows, offsetToken='1000')# reopen channel; resume after latest committed token

Snowpipe Streaming persists an application-supplied offset token with committed rows on a named channel. On reopen, read the latest token and replay retained source data after it. This is not a direct equivalent of Auto Loader's per-micro-batch file limit: client batching, channels, buffering, and source retention control capacity. High-performance channels can be cleared after 30 days without ingestion, so keep a separate offset when that matters.

title: CompletionService returns the fastest finished task—not the first submitted
goal: Consume concurrent Java results in completion order without blocking behind a slow task submitted first.
concept:
Three cooks receive tickets in order A, B, C. C finishes first. Reading the ticket stack in submission order makes everyone wait for A; reading the pickup shelf uses work as it finishes.

ExecutorCompletionService runs tasks on an executor and places each completed Future on a completion queue. take() waits for the next completed task. It does not promise submission order. Keep the returned futures if you may need cancellation.
example: Requests A, B, and C sleep for 90, 40, and 10 milliseconds. They are submitted A then B then C. The completion queue yields C, B, A.

use_case.when: Use a completion service when many independent calls may finish out of order and results can be processed immediately.
use_case.example: A Java metadata fan-out queries three regions and streams each completed inventory result to an aggregator.
use_case.decision: Use invokeAll when submission-order results and all-task completion are clearer. Use structured concurrency when your supported JDK and lifecycle policy fit; JDK 25's API remains preview.

practice: Switch between completion order and submission-order Future.get calls. Predict which result blocks the consumer first.
boundary: The Java run uses fixed sleeps and three successful tasks. It omits failures, timeouts, cancellation, executor saturation, backpressure, ordering requirements, and distributed side effects.

submit A(90), B(40), C(10)
'+(q?'take C at 10ms':'wait for A until 90ms')+'
'+(q?'then B, A':'then B, C already done')+'
';};completionMode.onchange=paintCompletion;paintCompletion();

title: Route routine changes automatically; reserve approval meetings for real risk
goal: Reduce decision delay by matching approval depth to evidence-based change risk.
concept:
An airport does not send every traveler to the same inspection room. Known low-risk cases follow a fast standard path; unusual risk gets deeper review.

A single architecture board for every change creates a queue even when automated tests and team ownership already control routine work. The senior-leadership move is not “remove governance.” It is to define risk classes, automate evidence for normal changes, name the exceptional decider, and measure approval wait separately from implementation time.
example: Ten weekly changes reach a board. Eight are routine and wait three days; two change regulated data boundaries and deserve review. Risk routing removes 24 routine queue-days while retaining the two high-risk decisions.

use_case.when: Use risk-tiered approval when teams repeatedly wait for an external board on changes with known controls.
use_case.example: Data-product schema additions with passing compatibility tests take the fast path; cross-account PII sharing requires security and data-owner review.
use_case.decision: Define observable risk signals, required evidence, escalation owners, and audit sampling. Do not let teams self-label high-risk work as routine without controls.

practice: Switch between one board for all ten changes and a risk-routed path. Predict routine queue-days.
boundary: The calculator assumes fixed three-day waits and perfect classification. It omits false negatives, correlated risk, audit cost, regulatory mandates, meeting capacity, and the value of expert review.

title: Use form elicitation for preferences; send secrets to a URL flow
goal: Keep passwords, API keys, payments, and OAuth credentials out of MCP form responses and model context.
tag: GenAI engineering · harness engineering · MCP elicitation
concept:
A waiter can ask “window or aisle?” at the table. A credit-card PIN belongs in the bank's secure terminal, not spoken into the dining room.

MCP form elicitation returns structured, non-sensitive answers through the client and into the tool conversation. Sensitive information must use URL mode or another out-of-band flow. In the 2026-07-28 lifecycle, the request can arrive through multi-round-trip input-required flow, but the security boundary remains: form content is in-band.
example: Tool deploy59 asks for region and maintenance window in a form. When it needs cloud authorization, it returns a trusted HTTPS URL. The harness shows the destination, waits for completion, and never copies the credential into form JSON.

use_case.when: Use elicitation when a long-running tool needs a small user decision it cannot infer safely.
use_case.example: A deployment tool asks for region in form mode, then opens the organization's OAuth approval URL.
use_case.decision: Classify every requested field. Use form only for non-sensitive structured data. Validate URL origin, explain the transition, require explicit user action, and bind completion to the original request.

practice: Classify a region choice and an API key. Watch the harness route one in-band and one out-of-band.
boundary: The model classifies two fields. It does not implement MCP transport, MRTR, URL-origin policy, OAuth, phishing defense, callback binding, client capability negotiation, or secret storage.

title: Pair a 2D n-transistor with a 1D p-transistor to build complementary logic
goal: Understand what mixed-dimensional CMOS demonstrated and keep device results separate from manufacturing readiness.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · low-dimensional electronics · research deep dive
concept:
A two-person saw works because one person pulls each direction. Complementary logic similarly pairs an n-type path that pulls output low with a p-type path that pulls output high.

A Nature Electronics paper combines two-dimensional single-crystal MoS₂ n-type transistors with one-dimensional aligned carbon-nanotube p-type transistors. The reported inverters show rail-to-rail operation, peak static power below 1 pW, and 19 ps single-stage delay. The team also reports logic gates, a 4-bit adder, and SRAM-like cells. These are device and circuit demonstrations, not a production process.
example: For an inverter, input 0 turns the p-side path on and output rises to 1. Input 1 turns the n-side path on and output falls to 0. The material pairing supplies opposite carrier types in one complementary circuit.

use_case.when: Study this work when evaluating post-silicon complementary device integration and ultra-low-power logic research.
use_case.example: A research roadmap compares low-dimensional transistor stacks for edge logic or dense experimental memory.
use_case.decision: Use the paper as evidence for integrated circuit function. Before product comparison, require yield, variability, contacts, endurance, thermal behavior, interconnect, area, fabrication throughput, and standardized workload data.

practice: Toggle the inverter input and watch the active pull-up or pull-down path. Then identify what the binary toy omits.
boundary: The model is an ideal Boolean inverter. It does not reproduce device physics, voltage transfer curves, the reported 19 ps measurement, static power, SRAM margins, variability, fabrication, or scaling.

title: fail-fast cancels sibling matrix jobs; continue-on-error forgives only one job
goal: Model GitHub Actions matrix failures so experimental coverage does not hide stable-platform breakage.
tag: CI/CD & GitHub Actions · testing · matrix failure policy
concept:
A fire alarm can evacuate the whole building, while a test-kitchen mistake can be recorded without closing the restaurant. These are different policies.

In a job matrix, strategy.fail-fast applies to the matrix and defaults to true: a non-forgiven failure cancels queued and in-progress siblings. continue-on-error applies to one job. Mark only the experimental combination as allowed to fail; do not apply it to stable coverage.
example: Java 21 and 25 are required; Java 26-ea is experimental. If 26-ea fails with continue-on-error: true, stable jobs continue. If Java 21 fails, fail-fast cancels siblings.

use_case.when: Use a test matrix when one codebase supports multiple runtimes or operating systems.
use_case.example: A data connector tests supported JDKs and one early-access JDK without letting the experiment mask stable regressions.
use_case.decision: Keep required combinations un-forgiven. Label experiments explicitly, decide whether fast cancellation saves useful capacity, and retain enough logs to diagnose the first required failure.

practice: Switch the failing combination between experimental and stable. Predict which siblings are cancelled.
boundary: The model has three jobs and instant state transitions. It omits runner timing, cancellation races, queued capacity, retries, artifacts, billing, branch protection, and required-check naming.

title: maximum: 100 without type: number still allows the string ‘huge’
goal: Write OpenAPI 3.2 schemas whose constraints apply to the instance types you actually intend to accept.
concept:
A sign saying “maximum 100 kilograms” constrains weight. It says nothing about a box labeled with the word “huge.”

OpenAPI 3.2 Schema Objects use JSON Schema semantics. If a schema omits type, it allows all JSON types. A numeric keyword such as maximum applies to numbers but does not itself require the instance to be numeric. Add type: number when that is the contract.
example: The request field batchSize has only maximum: 100. Number 120 fails, number 80 passes, and string "huge" is not rejected by that numeric constraint. Adding type: integer rejects the string.

use_case.when: Use explicit types whenever an API contract relies on type-specific JSON Schema keywords.
use_case.example: An ingestion API limits batchSize to 100 but must reject strings before they reach scheduler code.
use_case.decision: Declare type, bounds, required properties, and object closure deliberately. Test the validator used at the gateway and server; documentation alone is not runtime enforcement.

practice: Toggle the explicit type and validate 80, 120, and the string huge.
boundary: The model implements only a tiny subset of JSON Schema. It omits dialect negotiation, integer versus number details, composition, null, coercion, formats, unevaluated properties, and validator differences.
